steps: Unpack & inspect
Check the stove and parts for transit damage and report missing parts to the dealer. Remove the packaging in the flue collar and above the baffle; don't damage the label or its cable when lifting.
Floor protection
Combustible floors need a noncombustible protector under and beyond the stove: 33in x 31-1/2in minimum (US), 43in x 40in (Canada). No insulated hearth pad or R-value required.
Set clearances
Position the stove per the Figure 4 table for the connector type and shield option (A–F, p. 10) and Figure 5 for the connector. Alcove: 51-3/4" min. width, 56" min. ceiling.
Outside air (if used)
Kit 96-53400 to a minimum 3" duct, terminated no higher than the stove's air intake. Required in mobile homes; in Canada add a 100% closing damper and fasten the stove to the floor.
Connector pipe
6" 24 or 25 MSG blued steel, crimped ends toward the stove, three sheet metal screws per joint, horizontal runs rising 1/4" per foot. Never through a floor, ceiling, attic or concealed space.

• Single wall: 6" (152 mm), at least 24 MSG or 25 MSG blued steel. No aluminum or galvanized pipe.
  • Double wall (rear pipe, to reduce clearances): Simpson Dura Vent DVL or Metalbestos DS recommended; Security, GSW and Ameritec also acceptable. The double wall clearances in this manual are for DuraVent DVL.
  • Crimped end toward the stove. Secure every joint, including the flue collar, with three #10 x 1/2" sheet metal screws in the pre-drilled holes.
  • As short and straight as possible; horizontal runs rise at least 1/4" per foot (21mm/m).
  • Through a combustible wall: a wall thimble or listed pass-through per NFPA Code 211 or CAN/CSA-B365. The four NFPA wall pass-through systems are described on p. 12.
  • Never through a floor, ceiling, attic or roof space, closet or similar concealed space. Never connect to air distribution ductwork.
Rear exit (if used)
Ships with a top flue. Swap the flue collar and flue plate (5/32" hex key, keep the ¼" gasket), cut the rear heat shield for the pipe and refit it. Needs a draft of -0.08" WC or more.

The Craftsbury ships in the vertical flue configuration.

Maker's website: Flue Exit Location Top. Install to the manual.

To convert to a rear flue:

  1. With a 5/32" hex key, remove the two screws inside the flue collar and remove the collar from the top.
  2. Loosen the two screws and lift off the rear heat shield.
  3. With the 5/32" hex key, remove the two screws and the flue plate from the back.
  4. Install the flue collar on the back and the flue plate on the top, 2 screws each. Keep the ¼" gasket in the channel of both for a sealed firebox.
  5. With metal snips, remove the section of the rear heat shield so the pipe can pass through.
  6. Re-install the shield with the two screws in its keyhole features and the standoffs behind it, then tighten.

Rear exit needs a draft of -0.08" WC or more. Don't use it without sufficient draft.

Note: for rear exit, p. 15 gives a minimum chimney height of 15'; p. 17 gives a recommended minimum of 19 feet off the floor (16 feet 7 1/4 inches from the top of the stove).
Connect to the chimney

Listed Type HT (2100° F) chimney per UL 103 or ULC S629, or a code-approved masonry chimney with a flue liner, not shared with any other appliance. 6" ID flue for new installs; an existing 8" flue with a reducer.

• Chimney size: not less than the flue collar, nor more than three times its cross-sectional area. Masonry: maximum 6" diameter or 8" x 8" tile for best results.
  • Have a professional check a masonry chimney for cracks, loose mortar, deterioration and blockage first; the cleanout door must close and seal tightly.
  • Flue liners: tile with a minimum 5/8" wall, refractory mortar and at least 1" air space; or a UL listed 6" stainless steel liner, insulated or wrapped (or the space filled with vermiculite).
  • Interior chimney: at least 2" to combustibles, fire stops at floors and ceilings, insulation at least 2" away. Exterior chimney: at least 1" to combustibles.
  • Prefabricated chimney: use the same maker's pass-through, tee, fire-stops, insulation shield, flashing and cap, and follow its instructions exactly. A cleanout tee is recommended.
Chimney height & draft check
At least 3 feet above the roof opening and 2 feet above any roof within 10 feet. Check the draft at installation: -0.06" to -0.1" WC; above -0.1" WC fit a stovepipe damper.

Min. height, top exit16 feet (4.9 m) off the floor or 13 feet 7 1/4 inches (4.3 m) from the top of the stove
Min. height, rear exit19 feet (5.8m) off the floor or 16 feet 7 1/4 inches (5.2m) from the top of the stove
Max. height30 feet (9m)

A stovepipe damper is generally not needed, but use one where the chimney height gives too much draft (above -0.1" WC).

Note: for rear exit, p. 15 gives a minimum chimney height of 15'; p. 17 gives a recommended minimum of 19 feet off the floor (16 feet 7 1/4 inches from the top of the stove).
Mobile home extras
Per 24 CFR Part 3280 (HUD): outside air kit, stove fastened to the floor with the shipping clips, and a listed mobile home chimney & connector kit with spark arrester. Never in a sleeping room.

• Install per 24 CFR, Part 3280 (HUD). An outside air kit is required.
  • Permanently attach the stove to the floor with the shipping clips and fasteners long enough to reach the subfloor.
  • Mobile Home Chimney & Connector Kit to UL103 or ULC-S629: stainless spark arrester cap, storm collar, adjustable vented flashing 0/12 – 6/12, two 24" chimney pipes, 24" support box with built-in starter section and trim.
  • Chimney attached directly to the stove, at least 3 feet above the roof it passes through and 2 feet above any part of the home within 10 feet. Terminations removable at or below 13-1/2 feet above ground without special tools; chimney mechanically secured to the ceiling support box.
  • Chimney exiting other than through the roof, 7 feet or less above ground: guard or enclose it up to 7 feet.
  • Spark arrester net free area at least 4 times the net area of the chimney outlet; openings must stop a ½ inch sphere and pass a 3/8" sphere.
  • Remove the chimney when the home is transported.
Do not install in a sleeping room in a mobile home. Maintain the structural integrity of the walls, floor, ceiling and roof.

panels.title: Stove smokes
items: Operating technique → fully open the primary air one minute before opening the door, with the bypass open
Cold chimney or reverse draft → preheat the chimney; briefly open a window in the room
Bypass not closed → close it once the catalysts are in the active range
Oversized, undersized or short chimney → reline; draft inducer or new chimney; lengthen it
Air leaks or more than one appliance on the flue → seal connections, check clean-out doors, disconnect other appliances

panels.title: Uncontrolled or short burn
items: Door not sealed, or air leaking at the glass gasket → close tightly; replace gaskets
Excessive draft → operate at low burn; correct draft over 0.1 WC with stovepipe damper(s)
Extra-long or oversized chimney → shorten it or add damper(s); reline to the proper diameter
High winds or hilltop location → install a chimney cap

panels.title: Insufficient heat
items: Green or low-Btu wood → air-dried wood, preferably dried at least one year
Low burn rate → operate the stove at a higher burn rate
Cold exterior chimney → reline or insulate the chimney
Leaky stovepipe or chimney → check the installation; insulated prefab or properly sized masonry chimney
Too much heat loss from the house → insulate, seal windows and openings

panels.title: Catalyst problems
items: Fly ash on the catalysts → brush the cold combustor softly or vacuum; no cardboard, gift wrap or garbage; don't close the bypass too soon
Plugging from wet or pitchy wood → burn dry wood; reach light-off before closing the bypass; a hot fire held in the upper range for one hour may burn it off
Warping or bowing from long hot periods → lower the air setting to keep catalyst temperatures in range

light.title: Lighting a fire
light.html:
Once your stove is broken in, start every fire this way:

  1. Open the bypass handle (pointed toward the front of the stove). Open the front door.
  2. Put five or six double sheets of tightly twisted newspaper in the center of the firebox. Stand about 10 pieces of kindling over it like a tee-pee, each about 1/2" thick and 10" to 16" long.
  3. Fully open the primary air control by pulling the lever all the way out.
  4. Light the paper. Leave the door slightly open until the kindling catches and the draft starts to pull, then close it.
  5. Once the kindling is burning, add logs, small ones first. Keep them away from the glass.
  6. When the fire is burning well and the catalyst thermometer shows the active range, close the bypass handle.
  7. Run on a high setting for about 20 minutes, then set your burn rate with the air control.

Reloading

Open the bypass before you open the door. Open the door a crack, pause, then open it fully so the smoke clears. Reload on a bed of hot, red coals. If the fire was cool or down to charcoal, run at medium to high for about 10 minutes before closing the bypass again.

Never use gasoline, kerosene, charcoal lighter fluid or similar liquids to start or freshen up a fire.

breakin.title: Breaking in a new stove
breakin.html:
Soapstone has to be seasoned: its natural moisture must be driven out slowly, and the furnace cement must cure. Over-firing a new stove can crack the soapstone. Build your first fire, and the first fire of every season, like this:

  1. Open the bypass handle and the front door. Put five or six double sheets of tightly twisted newspaper in the center, with about ten pieces of kindling crisscrossed on top.
  2. Fully open the primary air control by pulling the handle toward you.
  3. Light the paper. Leave the door slightly open until the kindling burns and the draft pulls.
  4. Close the door and let the fire burn.
  5. Keep a steady, low-heat fire. The stove should get warm, but not hot to the touch. Add a few small chunks of wood at most.
  6. Once it is warm but not hot, push the air control fully in and let the fire die out completely.
  7. Let the stove return to room temperature.
Too hot: visible steam, boiling moisture or hissing mean the soapstone is too hot.

Smoke and smells are normal at first while the paint and oils cure; open a few windows. A dark liquid may drip onto the hearth, so set foil around each leg for now. Cool break-in fires can build creosote fast, so check the stovepipe and chimney afterward.

bypass.title: The bypass and catalyst thermometer
bypass.html:
Your Craftsbury burns its smoke in a catalytic combustor. The bypass handle sends the smoke around the combustor or through it.

Handle toward the frontBypass open: smoke goes around the combustor
Handle toward the rearBypass closed: smoke goes through the combustor

Keep the bypass open when you start a fire and whenever you open the door. Close it once the combustor is active, and keep it closed while the stove burns in that range.

Reading the thermometer

  • Inactive: leave the bypass open until the stove heats up.
  • Active: close the bypass. The stove typically runs between 800 °F and 1300 °F.
  • Too Hot: keep the door closed, fully close the air control, and let the stove cool until the thermometer is back in Active.

Once active, the burning smoke keeps the combustor hot as long as there is wood in the stove. You should see little to no smoke from the chimney.

air.title: Air control, burn rates and over-firing
air.html:
The primary air lever sits under the ash lip. Pull it out for more air, a faster burn and more heat; push it in for a slower, cooler burn. It never closes completely.

Lowlever all the way in
Medium lowfrom low, pull out a little less than 1/4"
Medium highfrom low, pull out a little less than 3/8"
Highlever all the way out

Medium low is the typical setting and the better choice if you leave the stove unattended. Long periods on low build creosote, so run on high once or twice a day for 35 to 45 minutes to heat the stovepipe and chimney.

Signs of over-firing

Warped parts, short burn times, a roaring sound in the stove or stovepipe, or a discolored stovepipe. Too much draft, the wrong fuel, worn gaskets or an open door can cause it. If you suspect it, stop using the stove and call your dealer immediately.

Never over-fire your stove. It will damage the stove. Any sign of over-firing voids your warranty. Keep the door closed while the stove runs.

wood.title: Choosing firewood
wood.html:
Burn only natural firewood (cordwood). Air-dried, seasoned hardwood burns more efficiently and cleaner than softwood or green wood. Softwood burns hotter and faster; hardwood burns longer and makes better coals.

  • Season it: split, stack and air-dry green wood for a year. Seasoned wood is typically at or near 20% moisture; a hand-held moisture meter will tell you.
  • Store it: stack it on skids or blocks, off the ground, and cover only the top. Tarps over the sides trap moisture.
  • Don't store firewood within the stove's required clearances.
  • Never load ice-crusted wood into a burning stove.

Never burn

Garbage or trash, lawn clippings, coal, charcoal, pellets, artificial or wax logs, compressed wood, paper products (including colored or glossy paper), cardboard, plywood or particleboard, painted, treated (including pressure-treated), kiln-dried or unseasoned wood, driftwood (including salt-water driftwood) or other materials previously saturated with salt water, materials containing rubber (including tires), materials containing plastic, waste petroleum products, paints or paint thinners, solvents, asphalt products, materials containing asbestos, construction or demolition debris, railroad ties, manure or animal remains, highly volatile fuels or combustibles, or flammable fluids. Burning these materials may release toxic fumes, or make the stove ineffective and cause smoke. Using an unauthorized fuel such as coal could produce high levels of carbon dioxide in the living space, which at high levels could cause injury or death. Never use flammable fluids or chemicals to start a fire; they cause dangerous burning conditions in the stove. Keep all such materials away from the stove. Fire starters made of paper, cardboard, sawdust or wax are fine for lighting.

Wet wood means less heat, dirty glass and more creosote. The manual lists common woods by heat value on pages 22 and 23.

ash.title: Removing ashes
ash.html:
Empty the ashes at the end of every week, sooner if the firebox is full. You can leave a thin layer in the firebox if you like.

  1. Let the fire die down or go out completely.
  2. Push large live coals to the side and scoop out only the finer ash with a fireplace shovel.
  3. Put the ashes straight into a metal container with a tight-fitting lid. Nothing else goes in, and don't pour in water.
  4. Close the lid. Set the container on a noncombustible floor or on the ground outside, well away from anything that burns, liquid fuels and vehicles.
  5. Keep the ashes in the closed container until all the coals are thoroughly cool.
Coals in an ash bed can stay hot for several days. Never put ashes in wooden or plastic containers, trash cans or bags, and never set the container on a combustible surface or vinyl flooring.

Don't let ashes build up around the door opening. They can spill out, or pack into the gasket channel and stop the door from sealing.

glass.title: Cleaning the glass
glass.html:
The window is a tough, clear ceramic, not ordinary glass. Clean it only when the fire is out and the glass is cool.

  1. Dip a damp paper towel in gray ash and rub the inside of the glass in a circular motion.
  2. When the deposits are off, finish with window cleaner or a commercial stove-glass cleaner. Use the same cleaner on the outside.
  3. Wipe the cleaner off with a soft cloth or black-and-white newsprint.
No razor blades, steel wool or abrasives. Scratches and etching weaken the glass. Use only cleaners made for woodstoves.

Glass that always stays dirty means the stove runs too cool or the wood is wet. Keeping logs away from the glass helps the air-wash keep it clear.

Never run the stove with cracked or broken glass. Replace it right away with ceramic glass kit 93-58925 from your dealer.

Note: p. 31 says only a qualified service person should replace the glass panel; p. 32 says to wear work gloves and safety glasses if you replace it yourself.

care.title: Creosote and routine care
care.html:
Slow, cool fires give off tar and vapors that condense in the chimney as creosote. If it ignites, it burns extremely hot and can damage the chimney or even destroy the house.

Your routine

Every weekEmpty the ashes
Every other monthCheck the connector and chimney for creosote, do the dollar-bill test, brush fly ash and soot off the catalyst face
End of seasonTake apart and clean the connector, clean the chimney if needed, clean out the stove, check the catalyst and door gaskets

If creosote is building up, check at least monthly and remove it once it is more than 1/4" thick. A certified chimney sweep is recommended, plus a professional inspection before each heating season.

Prevent it: run with the air fully open for 35 to 45 minutes every day, and for 15 to 20 minutes after each reload.

Dollar-bill test: with the stove cool, shut the door on a dollar bill. If it pulls out with no resistance, adjust the latch or replace the gasket. Door gaskets need replacing every two to three seasons.

safety.title: Safety and chimney fires
safety.html:
If you have a chimney or stovepipe fire

  1. If the fire is too threatening, leave and call the fire department immediately.
  2. Otherwise, close the primary air control.
  3. Close the stovepipe damper, if you have one.
  4. Close the bypass (handle toward the rear).
  5. Keep the front door closed.
Never throw water on the stove, stovepipe or chimney. It can flash to steam and cause serious injury. Let the fire die out completely, then have the stove, stovepipe and chimney inspected and any damage fixed before you light it again.

Everyday safety

  • The stove is hot while it runs. Keep children and pets away.
  • Keep furniture, drapes, clothing and other combustibles at least 36" from the stove.
  • Keep the front door closed except to start the fire and reload.
  • Install smoke and CO detectors throughout the home, and keep an "A B C" rated fire extinguisher handy.
  • Never modify the stove or connect it to a flue used by another appliance.

warranty.title: Warranty at a glance
warranty.html:
Hearthstone covers defects in material or workmanship for the original retail purchaser of a stove installed by an authorized Hearthstone dealer (or its designated representative), from the original invoice date. It is not transferable. "Limited Lifetime" means 10 years.

Stone; cast iron not listed elsewhereLimited Lifetime
Door handles and latches; steel and firebox5 years
Enamel finish, glass, accessories1 year

Other parts are in the grid on p. 39. Labor is paid only in the first year, and only for a dealer-installed stove.

Catalysts are covered by their maker, Applied Ceramics: free replacement if one stops working within two years, then prorated prices from $130.00 (year 3) to $160.00 (year 6).

Note: the manual gives the catalyst free-replacement period as two (2) years, then refers to one replacement catalyst for each defective catalyst returned "during the three year period" (both on p. 38).

Not covered

  • Over-firing, such as warped or rust-colored cast iron
  • Not following the manual or local codes
  • Normal wear on gaskets, paint, baffles and glass

specOutput.title: Heat output
specOutput.html:
Maximum heat output40,000 BTUs per hour of cordwood
Heated areaup to a maximum of 1,400 square feet
Burn timeup to 16+ hrs. (Heat Life™: up to 20 hours)
Maker's website: HeatLife 16 Hours of heat.

Maximum output is based on independent laboratory test results. Insulation, windows, floor plan, stove placement and fuel quality can reduce the area heated. Wood per cubic foot of firebox varies from 10 to 25 lbs. with species, moisture and packing. The manual says not to treat the stove as the home's primary heat source.

Terminate the duct at the same level as, or lower than, the stove's air intake; the IRC does not allow it higher than the appliance. Site it where snow or leaves can't block it, screen it with ¼" x ¼" mesh and fit a rain/wind proof hood.

Canada: a damper allowing 100% closure, and the stove fastened to the floor with the shipping clips. Mobile homes: outside air is required. Consider it for tight houses, exhaust fans, smoke roll-out or back-drafting.

review.notes: Wall/corner clearances (Figure 4, p. 10, dimensions A–F) and connector clearances (Figure 5, p. 11, A/B) are keyed to letters defined only in the drawings, and the extracted table's E/F column order is ambiguous in the first row, so the values were not transcribed; the drawer points to the figures. For the same reason the catalog clearances_note (side 14", rear 16"/13¾"/9¾", corner 14"/7") could not be checked against the manual, though those numbers all appear in the p. 10 table. Floor-protector extension (Figure 3, p. 9), trim/mantel clearances (Figure 6, p. 13), chimney height (Figure 9, p. 17), typical chimney configurations (Figure 10, p. 18) and acceptable catalyst distortion (Figure 21, p. 30) exist only as figures and were not transcribed. Warranty grid (p. 39) is a check-mark table: only rows marked in all three fuel columns (wood/gas/pellet) were used; rows with one or two marks (clean burning air supply system, refractory/vermiculite panels/baffles, ash grate, burner, burn pot) are ambiguous in the text and left to the PDF. Coverage periods were read with each period label applying to the rows below it. P. 22 calls the stove "Craftsbury Model 8640"; everywhere else it is Model 8392. Kindling length metric differs: 10" to 16" is (254 mm to 457 mm) on p. 24 but (254 mm to 406 mm) on p. 25; the guide uses inches only. The 4" duct adaptor kit number is printed split across lines as "KIT #90- 53308" on p. 13. The troubleshooting chart (p. 34) says to empty the "ash pan"; the ash section (p. 27) describes shovel removal, which the guide follows.
